tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.

NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

53	
54	**A person.** Two independent sources tying the person to the role. If a namesake exists, say which one you rejected and why.
55

57

59	# <note code> <title> (agent: <model>, 2026-11-13)
60	
61	## Digest
62	(400 words at most: the 12 facts that matter most for deciding what to build tonight, each with its fact ID; 3 surprises; anything that contradicts the starting leads in section 7.)
63	
64	## Findings
65	(grouped under the key questions in your task)
66	
67	## NOT FOUND / NOT SEARCHED
68	
69	Searches used: N
70	```

73	
74	The coordinator's unverified starting ideas. Look for evidence against them as hard as evidence for them.
75	
76	1. Programmes that change the treatment from home readings (dose titration, protocol steps) improve outcomes; monitoring and reminders alone mostly do not.
77	2. In India the binding limit is the prescriber's time and the gap between visits, so the workable design keeps a doctor or health worker approving each change while software does the reading, the protocol logic and the drafting.
78	3. Candidate loops: (a) home blood-pressure readings driving a stepwise medicine protocol; (b) fasting-glucose readings driving insulin dose changes in type 2 diabetes; (c) an inhaler or breathing sensor plus air-quality data adapting an asthma or COPD plan; (d) phone-camera and pulse-sensor rehabilitation that adapts each session.
79	4. The durable advantage is outcome data, clinical validation and distribution, not the app.
80	5. The honest regulatory route is decision support with clinician sign-off first; autonomous dosing needs a licence later.
81	
82	## 8. Style
83	
84	Dense, factual, plain words, short sentences. No marketing language. No em dashes. Rupees with Indian grouping (₹1,200; ₹844 crore). Give US dollar figures as published.

29	  - PubMed: `https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=...` or `https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=json&term=...` then `esummary.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=json&id=...`
30	  - Europe PMC: `https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=...&format=json`
31	  - ClinicalTrials.gov: `https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=...`
32	  - openFDA devices: `https://api.fda.gov/device/510k.json?search=...`
33	  - arXiv: `http://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=...`
34	  - regulator pages, company pages, journal pages, GitHub.
35	- Blocked or limited: reddit.com (use the Arctic Shift API sparingly), LinkedIn, X and Instagram (search snippets only; never reconstruct a post you could not read).
36	- End the note with `Searches used: N`.
37	
38	## 4. The fact rule (the most important rule)
39	
40	- Every fact is one bullet or table row with: an ID (`<note code>-F<number>`, for example `D1-03-F12`), the value with its unit, the year the value refers to, the source URL, the date of the source item (or "undated"), and OPENED (you opened the page and saw the value) or SNIPPET (search snippet only).
41	- Open the primary source for every number that matters. A SNIPPET number is second class and must be labelled.
42	- Quotes: 25 words or fewer, verbatim, only from a page you opened.
43	- Your own memory is a lead, never a source. The leads in your task are also only leads: confirm each one or mark it NOT FOUND.
44	- Figures that conflict: record both, with dates and sources. Do not pick one.
45	- Tag each fact: CITED (published figure, source opened), THEIR CLAIM (a company says it about itself), OUR ARITHMETIC (you computed it; show the sum), SOURCE ESTIMATE (the source itself estimates or models), SNIPPET.
46	- Time-sensitive facts (prices, laws, funding, whether a company is alive) carry their date.
47	
48	## 5. Schemas
49	
50	**A study.** Name and year; design (randomised trial, cluster trial, cohort, review); size; country and setting; who was compared with whom; primary outcome; effect with its confidence interval or p value; length of follow-up; funder; main limits; URL. Record null and negative results as carefully as positive ones. Flag India and other low-resource evidence.
51	
52	**A company, product or programme.** What it is in one line; country; what it measures (device or biomarker); what it changes in the therapy; adaptive depth 0-4; who is in the loop (doctor, nurse, coach, nobody); evidence (trial? peer-reviewed? own data only?); regulatory status; price to the patient or payer; funding (amount, date, lead investor, or participant only); traction (THEIR CLAIM, with date); status as of Nov 2026 (alive, acquired, pivoted, shut); URL.
53	
54	**A person.** Two independent sources tying the person to the role. If a namesake exists, say which one you rejected and why.
55	
56	## 6. Note layout
57	
58	```
59	# <note code> <title> (agent: <model>, 2026-11-13)
60	
61	## Digest
62	(400 words at most: the 12 facts that matter most for deciding what to build tonight, each with its fact ID; 3 surprises; anything that contradicts the starting leads in section 7.)
63	
64	## Findings
65	(grouped under the key questions in your task)
66	
67	## NOT FOUND / NOT SEARCHED
68	
69	Searches used: N
70	```
71	
72	## 7. Starting leads to break
73	
74	The coordinator's unverified starting ideas. Look for evidence against them as hard as evidence for them.
75	
76	1. Programmes that change the treatment from home readings (dose titration, protocol steps) improve outcomes; monitoring and reminders alone mostly do not.
77	2. In India the binding limit is the prescriber's time and the gap between visits, so the workable design keeps a doctor or health worker approving each change while software does the reading, the protocol logic and the drafting.
78	3. Candidate loops: (a) home blood-pressure readings driving a stepwise medicine protocol; (b) fasting-glucose readings driving insulin dose changes in type 2 diabetes; (c) an inhaler or breathing sensor plus air-quality data adapting an asthma or COPD plan; (d) phone-camera and pulse-sensor rehabilitation that adapts each session.
79	4. The durable advantage is outcome data, clinical validation and distribution, not the app.
80	5. The honest regulatory route is decision support with clinician sign-off first; autonomous dosing needs a licence later.
81	
82	## 8. Style
83	
84	Dense, factual, plain words, short sentences. No marketing language. No em dashes. Rupees with Indian grouping (₹1,200; ₹844 crore). Give US dollar figures as published.
85

1	# D4-04 Why each safety check exists (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-14)
2	
3	## Digest
4	
5	The 12 facts that matter most:
6	
7	1. Creatinine rises on an ARB because blocking angiotensin II relaxes the efferent arteriole, so filtration pressure falls; the rise comes in the first 2 weeks and settles by 2 to 4 weeks (D4-04-F26, F27).
8	2. Accepted rise: under 30% creatinine (or 25% eGFR fall) continue and recheck; 30% or more look for dehydration or NSAIDs, then stop or reduce; no trial tested the cut-off (F21, F23, F27).
9	3. Rises below 30% still carry graded risk: death IRR 1.15 at 10-19%, 1.35 at 20-29% (UK, 122,363 people) (F22).
10	4. Recheck creatinine and potassium 1 to 2 weeks (NICE, UKKA) or 2 to 4 weeks (KDIGO) after starting or raising an ARB; the Indian IHCI sheets ask for no recheck (F23, F27, F34, F57).
11	5. Potassium: caution above 5.0 before starting; 5.5-5.9 recheck within 3 days; 6.0-6.4 within 1 day and stop the RAS blocker; 6.5 or more admit. Potassium sets the heart cell resting potential; the ECG can look normal (F24, F34, F35).
12	6. RAS blockers in the 2nd and 3rd trimester stop fetal urine, so the amniotic sac drains: lung hypoplasia, skull and limb deformities, death (F02, F54, F56). Stop within 2 working days; use labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa (F29, F30).
13	7. The first-trimester malformation signal (RR 2.71) shrinks to OR 1.14 against untreated hypertensive mothers (F31, F32).
14	8. Thiazide hyponatraemia: 2-year incidence 3.5-3.8%; HR about 4 in the first 30 days, 1.3 after a year; worse with age and low weight (F58, F61).
15	9. Chlorthalidone gives more hypokalaemia than HCTZ (6.0% vs 4.4%), no outcome gain; thiazide cardiac arrest risk rises with dose (F33, F37).
16	10. Amlodipine edema: 3.0% at 5 mg, 10.8% at 10 mg; arteriolar-only dilation raises capillary pressure; adding a RAS blocker cuts it 38% (F11, F65, F66).
17	11. Orthostatic hypotension affects about 22% of community elders (Kerala 9.6%), falls OR 1.73; hip fractures rise 43% in the 45 days after starting any antihypertensive; home self-testing works (kappa 0.90) (F39, F40, F42, F48, F50).
18	12. 180/110 without symptoms: 0-0.5% MACE at 7 days; emergency means organ damage; chronic hypertension shifts brain autoregulation upward, so crashing pressure is the danger (F68, F70, F72).
19	
20	Surprises: US labels give no numeric creatinine or potassium thresholds (F04, F06, F15); thiazide hyponatraemia is far commoner than labels say (F58); intensive targets do not raise orthostatic hypotension (F44), but the weeks after starting do (F48).
21	
22	## What this suggests for the product
23	
24	- Suggestion: schedule a creatinine and potassium test 1 to 2 weeks after telmisartan starts and after 40 to 80 mg, and block the next step-up until it is back (F23, F27, F34, F57).
25	- Suggestion: encode the creatinine rule as a trend (percent change from the pre-telmisartan value), not pass or fail: under 30% continue and recheck; 30% or more goes to the doctor with a dehydration and NSAID checklist (F21, F22, F23, F27).
26	- Suggestion: encode potassium bands with recheck windows (5.5-5.9 in 3 days, 6.0-6.4 in 1 day, 6.5 urgent), and ask about potassium-based "low sodium" salt and painkillers before telmisartan (F07, F28, F34).
27	- Suggestion: a pregnancy and contraception question every cycle for women of childbearing age on or about to start telmisartan or chlorthalidone; "pregnant" triggers a stop-within-2-working-days alert and a drafted switch for the doctor (F01, F29, F30, F57).
28	- Suggestion: for patients 60 and over, add a sit-then-stand reading pair (1 and 3 minutes) plus a dizziness and falls question in the 45 days after each step; a 20/10 drop flags the doctor (F38, F41, F48, F50).
29	- Suggestion: sodium test within the first month of chlorthalidone, prioritised for older, thin patients and the hot season (F58, F61, F62).
30	- Suggestion: ask about ankle swelling after the amlodipine 10 mg step and send it to the doctor as a reason to move to the telmisartan step rather than stop (F11, F65, F66).
31	- Suggestion: a reading of 180/110 or more triggers a rested repeat and a symptom checklist (chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, vision, weakness): symptoms go to same-day care; no symptoms go to urgent doctor review, never extra doses to bring it down fast (F68, F70, F71, F72).
32	
33	## Findings
34	
35	### Labels (US DailyMed): what each label says and why
36	
37	- D4-04-F01 | Telmisartan boxed warning: fetal toxicity | Boxed warning: "When pregnancy is detected, discontinue telmisartan as soon as possible." and "Drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus". Generic telmisartan label (Ascend/Alkem, made in India), revised March 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03, SPL 2026-11-04 | OPENED | CITED
38	- D4-04-F02 | Why RAS blockers harm the fetus (label mechanism and timing) | Label 5.1: RAS-acting drugs "during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy reduces fetal renal function and increases fetal and neonatal morbidity and death". Chain: less fetal urine, so oligohydramnios, so fetal lung hypoplasia and skeletal deformations; neonatal skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension, renal failure, death. Label 8.1: most first-trimester studies did not separate RAS drugs from other antihypertensives. If no alternative: serial ultrasound of the amniotic environment. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
39	- D4-04-F03 | Losartan carries the same fetal warning | Cozaar label 5.1 uses the same wording as telmisartan (2nd and 3rd trimester, oligohydramnios, lung hypoplasia, skull hypoplasia, anuria, death; discontinue as soon as possible). Year 2021 label text. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=9949448f-c3b9-44ee-94ed-c1aca8c90f39 | label revised 2021-06, SPL 2026-01-21 | OPENED | CITED
40	- D4-04-F04 | Telmisartan and the kidney (label) | Label 5.5: "As a consequence of inhibiting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, anticipate changes in renal function in susceptible individuals." Patients whose filtration depends on RAAS (severe heart failure, renal dysfunction) can get oliguria, progressive azotaemia, rarely acute renal failure or death. In ACE-inhibitor studies of unilateral or bilateral renal artery stenosis, creatinine or urea rose; "anticipate an effect similar" with telmisartan. The label gives no numeric creatinine threshold and no recheck interval. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
41	- D4-04-F05 | Telmisartan creatinine rise in trials is rare | Label 6.1: a creatinine rise of 0.5 mg/dL or more in 0.4% on telmisartan against 0.3% on placebo; one patient stopped for creatinine and urea rise. In 30 hypertensive patients with normal kidneys on telmisartan 80 mg (with or without HCTZ 12.5 mg) for 8 weeks: no clinically significant change in renal blood flow, GFR, filtration fraction or creatinine clearance. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
42	- D4-04-F06 | Telmisartan potassium (label) | Label 5.3: hyperkalaemia "may occur in patients on ARBs", especially advanced renal impairment, heart failure, dialysis, potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium-containing salt substitutes. Advice: "Consider periodic determinations of serum electrolytes". No numeric threshold. Mechanism: ARB blocks angiotensin II at the AT1 receptor, so less aldosterone drive, so less potassium excreted by the collecting duct. Telmisartan multiple-dose studies: "no clinically significant changes" in serum potassium, sodium, glucose or uric acid. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
43	- D4-04-F07 | Low-salt substitutes are a potassium source | Telmisartan label names "potassium-containing salt substitutes" as a hyperkalaemia risk with ARBs (relevant in India where low-sodium salt with potassium chloride is promoted). Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
44	- D4-04-F08 | Losartan potassium and kidney advice (label) | Cozaar 5.4: "Monitor serum potassium periodically and treat appropriately. Dosage reduction or discontinuation of COZAAR may be required". Highlights: "Monitor renal function and potassium in susceptible patients." No numeric thresholds. RENAAL (1,513 type 2 diabetes with nephropathy): losartan cut sustained creatinine doubling by 25% and end-stage kidney disease by 29%, no effect on mortality. Year 2021 label. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=9949448f-c3b9-44ee-94ed-c1aca8c90f39 | label revised 2021-06 | OPENED | CITED
45	- D4-04-F09 | ARB low blood pressure: who is at risk | Telmisartan and losartan labels 5.2: symptomatic hypotension in patients with "an activated renin-angiotensin system, such as volume- or salt-depleted patients (e.g., those being treated with high doses of diuretics)". Mechanism: when salt and water are low, blood pressure leans on angiotensin II, so blocking it drops pressure more. Telmisartan label: dialysis patients "may develop orthostatic hypotension". A transient fall is not a contraindication. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
46	- D4-04-F10 | Telmisartan time course (label) | "Most of the antihypertensive effect is apparent within 2 weeks and maximal reduction is generally attained after 4 weeks." Response dose-related over 20 to 80 mg. Year 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=56a72ddf-c2a2-45ce-91b1-1fcfbff52c10 | label revised 2025-03 | OPENED | CITED
47	- D4-04-F11 | Amlodipine ankle swelling: dose dependence and frequency | Norvasc label 6.1 placebo-controlled trials, edema: 1.8% at 2.5 mg (n=275), 3.0% at 5 mg (n=296), 10.8% at 10 mg (n=268), placebo 0.6% (n=520). So the step from 5 mg to 10 mg (protocol step 2) roughly triples edema (OUR ARITHMETIC: 10.8 / 3.0 = 3.6). Dizziness 1.1/3.4/3.4% vs 1.5%; flushing 0.7/1.4/2.6% vs 0.0%; palpitation 0.7/1.4/4.5% vs 0.6%. Pfizer SPL 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=abd6a2ca-40c2-485c-bc53-db1c652505ed | SPL 2025-06-09 | OPENED | CITED
48	- D4-04-F12 | Amlodipine edema is more common in women | Norvasc label: edema 5.6% in men and 14.6% in women on amlodipine (all doses pooled), against 1.4% and 5.1% on placebo (n=1,218 men, 512 women on drug). Pfizer SPL 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=abd6a2ca-40c2-485c-bc53-db1c652505ed | SPL 2025-06-09 | OPENED | CITED
49	- D4-04-F13 | Amlodipine: sudden low pressure unlikely, heart rate unchanged | Norvasc 5.1: "Because of the gradual onset of action, acute hypotension is unlikely." Chronic dosing lowers supine and standing pressure without significant change in heart rate or plasma catecholamines. 5.2: worsening angina or MI can follow starting or raising the dose in severe obstructive coronary disease. Pfizer SPL 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=abd6a2ca-40c2-485c-bc53-db1c652505ed | SPL 2025-06-09 | OPENED | CITED
50	- D4-04-F14 | Amlodipine in pregnancy (label) | Norvasc 8.1: post-marketing data "are not sufficient to inform a drug-associated risk for major birth defects and miscarriage"; no adverse developmental effects in animal studies. No boxed warning. Pfizer SPL 2025. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=abd6a2ca-40c2-485c-bc53-db1c652505ed | SPL 2025-06-09 | OPENED | CITED
51	- D4-04-F15 | Chlorthalidone electrolytes (label) | Thalitone 5.3: can cause hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypochloraemic alkalosis, hypomagnesaemia; low magnesium makes low potassium "difficult to treat despite potassium repletion". "Monitor serum electrolytes periodically." Stop the drug if low potassium comes with muscle weakness, paresis or ECG changes. 12.2: "dose-related reductions in serum potassium levels, elevations in serum uric acid and blood glucose". No numeric thresholds or recheck interval. Label revised 12/2019. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=bc5a0299-115b-4e60-bb3f-c75a95c51c15 | label revised 2019-12, SPL 2026-06-26 | OPENED | CITED
52	- D4-04-F16 | Chlorthalidone uric acid, glucose, calcium (label) | Thalitone 5.4: may alter glucose tolerance; may raise cholesterol and triglycerides; raises uric acid "due to reduced clearance of uric acid" and may "precipitate gout in susceptible patients"; lowers urinary calcium so serum calcium can rise. Patient counselling lists signs of potassium loss: thirst, tiredness, drowsiness, restlessness, muscle cramps, nausea, vomiting, faster pulse. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=bc5a0299-115b-4e60-bb3f-c75a95c51c15 | label revised 2019-12 | OPENED | CITED
53	- D4-04-F17 | Chlorthalidone in pregnancy (label) | Thalitone 8.1: decades of observational data have not shown major birth defects or miscarriage, but "Chlorthalidone should not be used as first-line therapy to treat hypertension in pregnancy". Mechanism: thiazides cross the placenta (umbilical vein levels approach maternal plasma) and, like other diuretics, "can cause placental hypoperfusion"; neonatal jaundice, thrombocytopenia, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte problems reported. So the bar is softer than for ARBs (no boxed warning). https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=bc5a0299-115b-4e60-bb3f-c75a95c51c15 | label revised 2019-12 | OPENED | CITED
54	- D4-04-F18 | Chlorthalidone and the kidney, low pressure (label) | Thalitone 5.1-5.2: may cause symptomatic hypotension, more with impaired sympathetic response, volume depletion or salt restriction; diuretics can cause changes in renal function including acute renal failure, more in CKD, heart failure, volume depletion. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=bc5a0299-115b-4e60-bb3f-c75a95c51c15 | label revised 2019-12 | OPENED | CITED
55	- D4-04-F19 | Hydrochlorothiazide metabolic effects (label) | HCTZ label (Chartwell, rev. 07/2023): "Hyperuricemia may occur or acute gout may be precipitated"; "Hyperglycemia may occur with thiazide diuretics. Thus, latent diabetes mellitus may become manifest"; diabetics may need insulin or oral drug adjustment; raises urinary magnesium loss; may slightly raise serum calcium. Warning signs of fluid or electrolyte imbalance listed: dry mouth, thirst, weakness, lethargy, confusion, seizures, cramps, hypotension, oliguria, tachycardia. Orthostatic hypotension listed as an adverse reaction (worse with alcohol). https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=4e43dd27-3f4b-4205-a26e-6ecaa8281347 | label revised 2023-07 | OPENED | CITED
56	- D4-04-F20 | Hydrochlorothiazide in pregnancy (older-format label) | HCTZ label: "Routine use of diuretics during normal pregnancy is inappropriate and exposes mother and fetus to unnecessary hazard"; thiazides cross the placenta and appear in cord blood; risk of fetal or neonatal jaundice and thrombocytopenia. The same label also warns of non-melanoma skin cancer (sun protection) and acute angle-closure glaucoma within hours to weeks of starting. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=4e43dd27-3f4b-4205-a26e-6ecaa8281347 | label revised 2023-07 | OPENED | CITED
57	
58	### ARBs and the kidney: the creatinine rise, the 30% rule, when to recheck
59	
60	- D4-04-F21 | The 30% rule comes from Bakris and Weir 2000 | Review of 12 randomised trials (ACE inhibitor arms, n=1,102; average follow-up 3 years) in people with existing renal insufficiency: most showed an acute fall in GFR and rise in creatinine after starting. Conclusion: "acute increases in serum creatinine of up to 30% that stabilize within the first 2 months" of ACE-inhibitor therapy are strongly associated with long-term preservation of kidney function. Those with baseline creatinine 1.4 mg/dL or more had 55 to 75% risk reduction in renal progression. Note: ACE-inhibitor data, extended to ARBs by inference. Arch Intern Med 2000. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:10724055&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 10724055) | 2000-03 | OPENED | CITED
61	- D4-04-F22 | Disagreement: rises below 30% are not fully harmless (UK cohort) | Schmidt et al., BMJ 2017, UK CPRD 1997-2014, 122,363 people starting ACE inhibitor or ARB. 2,078 (1.7%) had creatinine rises of 30% or more; they were more often female, elderly, with heart or kidney disease, on NSAIDs, loop or potassium-sparing diuretics. Adjusted rate ratios for 30%+ rise against under 30%: end-stage renal disease 3.43 (2.40 to 4.91), MI 1.46 (1.16 to 1.84), heart failure 1.37 (1.14 to 1.65), death 1.84 (1.65 to 2.05). Graded: even 10-19% rise gave death IRR 1.15 (1.09 to 1.22) and 20-29% gave 1.35 (1.23 to 1.49) against under 10%. Observational, so the rise may mark sicker patients rather than cause harm. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:28279964&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 28279964, PMC5421447) | 2017-03 | OPENED | CITED
62	- D4-04-F23 | NICE NG203 recheck timing and thresholds for RAS blockers | NICE CKD guideline (published 25 Aug 2021, updated 24 Nov 2021), recs from 2008: 1.6.14 measure potassium and eGFR before starting and "between 1 and 2 weeks after starting renin-angiotensin system antagonists and after each dose increase". 1.6.19-1.6.20: do not change the dose if eGFR fall is under 25% or creatinine rise under 30%; repeat the test in 1 to 2 weeks. 1.6.21: if eGFR falls 25% or more or creatinine rises 30% or more, look for other causes (volume depletion, NSAIDs); if none, stop or reduce to a previously tolerated dose and add another drug. Scope: adults with CKD. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng203/chapter/Recommendations | 2021-11-24 | OPENED | CITED
63	- D4-04-F24 | NICE NG203 potassium thresholds for RAS blockers | 1.6.15: do not routinely start a RAS antagonist if pretreatment potassium "is greater than 5.0 mmol/litre". 1.6.18: stop RAS antagonists if potassium "increases to 6.0 mmol/litre or more" and other potassium-raising drugs have been stopped. 1.6.17: monitor more often if other potassium-raising drugs are co-prescribed. Scope: adults with CKD. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng203/chapter/Recommendations | 2021-11-24 | OPENED | CITED
64	- D4-04-F25 | NICE NG136 (hypertension) blood test after diuretic step | NG136 (published 28 Aug 2019, last updated 26 Feb 2026) 1.4.50: when adding further diuretic at step 4, "monitor blood sodium and potassium and renal function within 1 month of starting treatment". 1.4.49: low-dose spironolactone only if potassium is 4.5 mmol/l or less; 1.4.51 alpha- or beta-blocker if above 4.5. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations | 2026-02-26 | OPENED | CITED
65	- D4-04-F26 | Why creatinine rises on an ARB: the efferent arteriole (KDIGO mechanism) | KDIGO 2021 BP in CKD guideline, rationale to Practice Point 3.2.3: blocking angiotensin II "causes selectively greater vasodilatation of the efferent arterioles of the glomeruli, resulting in a decline of the intraglomerular filtration pressure", so GFR falls and creatinine rises. This is a pressure change, not tissue damage, which is why a small early rise is accepted and is reversible on stopping. RAS blockade also blunts aldosterone, so potassium tends to rise. Kidney Int 2021;99:S1-S87. https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/KDIGO-2021-BP-GL.pdf | 2021-03 | OPENED | CITED
66	- D4-04-F27 | KDIGO timing and the 30% rule | KDIGO 2021 Practice Point 3.2.3: check BP, creatinine and potassium "within 2-4 weeks of initiation or increase in the dose of a RASi"; for those at risk of hyperkalaemia, potassium before and at 1-2 weeks (expert opinion). Text: a creatinine rise "will typically happen during the first 2 weeks" and "should stabilize within 2-4 weeks in the setting of normal sodium and fluid intake"; shorter interval if baseline creatinine is high, potassium high-normal, or past hyperkalaemia. PP 3.2.5: "Continue ACEi or ARB therapy unless serum creatinine rises by more than 30% within 4 weeks". Other antihypertensives: gout HR 0.64 (0.49 to 0.86) against untreated hypertension. Mechanism per Thalitone label (F16): reduced renal clearance of uric acid. Arthritis Rheum 2012. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:22031222&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 22031222, PMC3253199) | 2012 | OPENED | CITED
127	- D4-04-F64 | Thiazide glucose rise tracks potassium loss | Quantitative review of 59 trials (83 thiazide arms, 1966-2004): weighted correlation between change in potassium and change in glucose r = -0.54 (-0.67 to -0.36), P<0.01. Proposed mechanism: low potassium reduces insulin secretion, so glucose rises; authors suggest correcting hypokalaemia may reverse it. Association across trial arms, not proof in individuals. Hypertension 2006. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:16801488&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 16801488) | 2006 | OPENED | CITED
128	
129	### Amlodipine ankle swelling (also F11, F12)
130	
131	- D4-04-F65 | Calcium-blocker edema: mechanism, frequency, time course, dose | Meta-analysis of 106 RCTs, 99,469 hypertensive patients. Mechanism stated: arteriolar dilatation causing "intracapillary hypertension and fluid extravasation" (the precapillary arteriole opens, the venous side does not, so capillary pressure rises and fluid leaks into the ankles). Weighted edema incidence 10.7% on calcium blockers vs 3.2% control; withdrawal for edema 2.1% vs 0.5%. Both rose with time on drug, reaching 24% and 5% after 6 months. High dose (over half the maximal dose) 16.1% vs low dose 5.7% (2.8 times). Dihydropyridines 12.3% vs non-dihydropyridines 3.1%. J Hypertens 2011. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:21558959&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 21558959) | 2011 | OPENED | CITED
132	- D4-04-F66 | Adding an ARB or ACE inhibitor reduces amlodipine edema | Meta-analysis of 25 RCTs, 17,206 patients, mean 9.2 weeks: calcium blocker plus RAS blocker had 38% less edema than calcium blocker alone, RR 0.62 (0.53 to 0.74); withdrawal for edema RR 0.38 (0.22 to 0.66). ACE inhibitors better than ARBs by indirect comparison (ratio of RR 0.74). Mechanism: RAS blockers dilate the venous (post-capillary) side, which lowers capillary pressure. Relevant to protocol step 3 (adding telmisartan to amlodipine 10 mg). Am J Med 2011. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:21295192&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 21295192) | 2011 | OPENED | CITED
133	
134	- D4-04-F67 | India: amlodipine pedal edema in practice | Mumbai hospital EMR study (Kokilaben Dhirubhai Ambani Hospital), 800 amlodipine and 800 cilnidipine monotherapy patients: pedal edema reported at some point in 23.9% on amlodipine and 27.6% on cilnidipine; 3.5% and 8.2% still had edema at study end. Retrospective, doses mixed; funding not stated in abstract. Int J Hypertens 2022. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:35251710&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 35251710, PMC8890895) | 2022 | OPENED | CITED
135	
136	### Very high readings: what 180/110 means
137	
138	- D4-04-F68 | 180/110 without symptoms: urgency, not emergency | Cleveland Clinic offices 2008-2013: 59,836 of 2,199,019 visits (4.6%) met hypertensive urgency (systolic 180 or more and/or diastolic 110 or more). Propensity-matched: 852 sent home vs 426 referred to hospital: MACE at 7 days 0 vs 2 (0.5%), 8-30 days 0 vs 2, 6 months 0.9% vs 0.9%. Hospital referral gave more admissions, no better outcomes; most still uncontrolled at 6 months (64.6% vs 66.6%). JAMA Intern Med 2016. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:27294333&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 27294333) | 2016 | OPENED | CITED
139	- D4-04-F69 | 180/110 marks a worse profile, risk runs through control | Campania Salute Network, Italy: 469 of 6,929 outpatients had urgency (180 and/or 110) at first visit; more often women, obese, diabetic, with LV hypertrophy and carotid plaque; 5-fold higher risk of uncontrolled BP in follow-up (4.1 to 6.8). CV events adjusted HR 1.42 (0.96 to 2.11), P=0.08: excess risk explained by later BP control and organ damage. Am J Hypertens 2020. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:31930302&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 31930302) | 2020 | OPENED | CITED
140	- D4-04-F70 | Emergency means acute organ damage, not a number | ESC Council on Hypertension 2019: hypertensive emergencies are very high BP "associated with acute organ damage" (heart, retina, brain, kidneys, large arteries) needing immediate but careful lowering; patients without acute organ damage "do not have a hypertensive emergency" and can usually take oral drugs and go home after brief observation. Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Pharmacother 2019. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:30165588&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 30165588) | 2019 | OPENED | CITED
141	- D4-04-F71 | NICE red flags at 180/120 | NG136 1.5.2: same-day specialist referral if clinic BP is 180/120 or more with retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, or "life-threatening symptoms such as new onset confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, or acute kidney injury". 1.5.1: without these, check for organ damage as soon as possible; repeat clinic BP within 7 days. Note NICE uses 120 diastolic; the Gujarat protocol and the US urgency definition (F68) use 110. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations | 2026-02-26 | OPENED | CITED
142	- D4-04-F72 | Why not to crash the pressure down: autoregulation shifts right | Strandgaard and Paulson 1995: brain blood flow is the same in hypertensive and normotensive people; "Chronic hypertension shifts the lower and upper blood pressure limits of CBF autoregulation towards higher pressure." Acute lowering cuts brain flow only below the lower limit; with chronic treatment autoregulation may re-adapt toward normal. So a long-standing hypertensive brain is used to high pressure; a sudden big drop can starve it, while very high pressure above the upper limit can push through and cause swelling (hypertensive encephalopathy). Neth J Med 1995. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:8538822&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 8538822) | 1995 | OPENED | CITED
143	- D4-04-F73 | Gradual intensive lowering raises brain blood flow in older people | RCT, 37 people over 70 (SBP over 150), 12 weeks, reviews every 2 weeks: intensive target under 130/80 lowered BP 26/17 mmHg and grey-matter blood flow rose 7 plus or minus 11 mL/min per 100 g (P=0.013); usual target (under 140/85) lowered 15/5 with no flow change. Supports slow, stepped lowering being safe for the brain. Hypertension 2013. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:23529166&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 23529166) | 2013 | OPENED | CITED
144	
145	
146	## NOT FOUND / NOT SEARCHED
147	
148	- NOT FOUND: any numeric creatinine or potassium threshold, or a recheck interval, in the US labels for telmisartan, losartan, chlorthalidone or HCTZ (all say "periodic" or "susceptible patients"; F04, F06, F08, F15). The numbers come from NICE, KDIGO and UKKA.
149	- NOT FOUND: a recheck of creatinine or potassium after starting telmisartan in the two IHCI state sheets opened (Telangana, Maharashtra; F57). The Gujarat HEARTS sheet itself was not opened in this note.
150	- NOT FOUND: losartan's urate-lowering effect in the Cozaar label text (label searched for "uric"; absent).
151	- NOT FOUND: a South Asian study of thiazide hyponatraemia risk factors (Hong Kong data used instead, F61); an Indian study of hyperkalaemia rates on telmisartan.
152	- NOT SEARCHED: ESH 2023, ACC/AHA 2017 and WHO 2021 text on lab monitoring, orthostatic testing and 180/110 (ISH 2020 page refused the fetch with HTTP 403).
153	- NOT SEARCHED: CDSCO-approved Indian telmisartan or chlorthalidone package inserts; Indian (FOGSI, ICMR) guidance on drugs in pregnancy; LASI national orthostatic hypotension prevalence.
154	- NOT SEARCHED: how fast potassium falls after starting a thiazide (days to weeks); sex breakdown of the Danish hyponatraemia cohort (abstract only, F58); mortality result of the TriNetX hyponatraemia cohort (F59, not in the part read).
155	- NOT SEARCHED: losartan-specific hyperkalaemia rates beyond the label; amlodipine edema by ancestry.

# D3-01 Claims check: D1-01 and D1-02 clinical evidence (agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-13)

## Verdict

Checked 53 fact IDs against the source (abstracts via NCBI E-utilities; PHTI PDFs; ResMed, AAFA, GOV.UK, SEC, ClinicalTrials.gov, trade pages). Status: CONFIRMED 48, CORRECTED 5, CONTESTED 0, NOT FOUND 0. Every number in the two notes matched its source. The corrections are precision fixes (a comparator, a date, a funder, a denominator), and five wordings in the Decision brief or DT1 need changing (listed under "Sentences to change"). Four SNIPPET facts were upgraded to OPENED: Propeller ceased operations, Teva Digihaler withdrawal, Rejoyn primary result, CRHCP incentives and free drugs.

Sentences to change in the Decision brief:
1. Tucker 6.1 mmHg: "with intensive co-interventions (titration by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling)", not "including dose changes".
2. STRONG-HF 15.2% vs 23.3%: adjusted, down-weighted Kaplan-Meier estimates at 180 days; high-intensity arm had four clinic visits and more adverse events (41% vs 29%).
3. "Telemonitoring without a therapy change" (TELE-HF, BEAT-HF): the abstracts do not show that. BEAT-HF had nurse "protocolized actions". Say "telemonitoring without a mandated dose protocol".
4. 3.3% at day 30: the median of 93 popular Android mental-health apps (2019), not "3.3% of users".
5. Rural China: add that the programme also gave discounted or free drugs and paid village doctors incentive supplements tied to control rates (now OPENED).

## Never say
- "Self-monitoring plus dose changes cut BP by 6.1 mmHg" (6.1 is any intensive co-intervention).
- "15.2% of patients against 23.3%" for STRONG-HF as if raw counts (raw: 74/506 and 109/502).
- "25% of Trivandrum heart-failure patients" (it is 25% of the 62% with reduced ejection fraction).
- "COBRA-BPS health workers changed doses" (they monitored and counselled; trained physicians treated).
- "Both heart-failure telemonitoring trials had no therapy change" (BEAT-HF protocolised actions).
- "Adherence rose from 30% to 84%" (two arms, not before and after).
- "3.3% of mental-health app users stay to day 30" (median app).
- "The China result is the protocol alone" (free or discounted drugs and incentives included).
- "Warfarin self-dosing beats self-testing" as a head-to-head result (separate trial sets, indirect).
- "Propeller shut down in <date>" (no date on the ResMed page); "ResMed closed Propeller purchase 31 Jan 2019" (press release is 7 Jan 2019).
- "PHTI says digital diabetes tools fail" without "non-continuous glucose monitor, type 2, US".

## Checks
| Fact ID | Claim as noted | Status | Verified value, source, date opened |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1-01-F01 | TASMINH2: 527 pts, 3.7 mmHg at 6 mo, 5.4 (2.4 to 8.5) at 12 mo; leg swelling 32% vs 22% | CONFIRMED | Primary is systolic change at 6 and 12 months, 1:1 vs usual care, 91% analysed, no imputation; funder UK Dept of Health programmes. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20619448/ (efetch, 13 Nov 2026). Patients had to be "willing to self-manage". |
| D1-01-F02 | TASMIN-SR: 552 pts, 9.2 (5.7 to 12.7) at 12 mo | CONFIRMED | Primary: systolic difference at 12-month office visit vs usual care; 450/552 (81%); multiple imputation 8.8. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25157723/ (13 Nov 2026) |
| D1-01-F03 | TASMINH4: -3.5 and -4.7; telemonitoring vs self-monitoring -1.2 NS; funder NIHR | CORRECTED | Numbers right (primary: clinic systolic at 12 months; 1,182 randomised, 1,003 analysed). Comparator is usual care titrated from clinic readings. Funding also includes Omron Healthcare UK. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29499873/ (13 Nov 2026) |
| D1-01-F04 | HyperLink: 57.2% vs 30.0%; -10.7 at 6 mo | CONFIRMED | Primary: control at both 6 and 12 months. Add: at 18 months (6 months after stopping) control was 71.8% vs 57.1%, so the percentage gap shrank to 14.7 points; systolic gap -6.6. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23821088/ (13 Nov 2026) |
| D1-01-F05 | Tucker: alone -1.0 (-3.3 to 1.2); intensive support -6.1; quote | CONFIRMED | 25 trials gave data, 15 trials / 7,138 for primary. Quote matches. "Co-interventions" = systematic titration by doctors, pharmacists or patients, education, or lifestyle counselling. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28926573/ (13 Nov 2026). Brief wording to fix (see Verdict). |
| D1-01-F06 | MedISAFE-BP: 0.5 mmHg, p=0.78, 411 pts | CONFIRMED | Co-primary outcomes: adherence (+0.4, p=0.01) and systolic (-0.5, -3.7 to 2.7, p=0.78); 412 randomised, 411 analysed; 12 weeks. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29710289/ (13 Nov 2026) |
| D1-01-F07 | HERB-DH1: -2.4 / -4.3 / -3.6 | CONFIRMED | Primary is 24 h ambulatory SBP, -2.4 (-4.5 to -0.3); untreated patients, vs lifestyle advice alone. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34455443/ (13 Nov 2026) |
| D1-01-F09 | CRHCP 18 mo: 57.0% vs 19.9%, -14.5 mmHg, 33,995 | CONFIRMED | Primary: BP <130/80 at 18 months; 8,865/15,414 vs 2,895/14,500; vs enhanced usual care; village doctors also coa

=== 10724055
1. Arch Intern Med. 2000 Mar 13;160(5):685-93. doi: 10.1001/archinte.160.5.685.

Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor-associated elevations in serum 
creatinine: is this a cause for concern?

Bakris GL(1), Weir MR.

Author information:
(1)Rush University Hypertension/Clinical Research Center, Department of 
Preventive Medicine, Rush Presbyterian-St Luke's Medical Center, Chicago, Ill 
60612, USA. gbakris@rush.edu

BACKGROUND: Reducing the actions of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system 
with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) slows nephropathy 
progression in patients with or without diabetes. Post hoc analyses of many 
ACEI-based clinical trials demonstrate the greatest slowing of renal disease 
progression in patients with the greatest degree of renal insufficiency at study 
initiation. However, many physicians fail to use ACEIs or angiotensin receptor 
blockers in patients with renal insufficiency for fear that either serum 
creatinine or potassium levels will rise.
OBJECTIVE: To determine if limited initial reduction in either glomerular 
filtration rate (GFR) or elevation in serum creatinine levels, associated with 
ACEI or angiotensin receptor blocker use, results in long-term protection 
against decline in renal function in patients with renal insufficiency.
METHODS: We reviewed 12 randomized clinical trials that evaluated renal disease 
progression among patients with preexisting renal insufficiency. Six of these 
studies were multicenter, double-blinded, and placebo controlled, with the 
remainder being smaller randomized studies with a minimum 2-year follow-up on 
renal function. These investigations evaluated patients with and without 
diabetes or systolic heart failure. Average duration of follow-up for all 
studies was 3 years. Trials were examined in the context of changes in either 
serum creatinine levels or GFR in the group randomized to an ACEI (N = 1,102). 
Sixty-four percent of these individuals (705/1,102) had renal function data at 
both less than 6 months and at the end of the study.
RESULTS: Most trials demonstrated that patients with preexisting renal 
insufficiency manifested an acute fall in GFR, a rise in serum creatinine, or 
both. Those randomized to an ACEI with a serum creatinine level of 124 pmol/L or 
greater (> or =1.4 mg/dL) demonstrated a 55% to 75% risk reduction in renal 
disease progression compared with those with normal renal function randomized to 
an ACEI. An inverse correlation was observed between the amount of renal 
function loss at baseline and the subsequent rate of annual decline in renal 
function following randomization to an antihypertensive regimen that contained 
an ACEI.
CONCLUSIONS: A strong association exists between acute increases in serum 
creatinine of up to 30% that stabilize within the first 2 months of ACEI therapy 
and long-term preservation of renal function. This relationship holds for 
persons with creatinine values of greater than 124 pmol/L (>1.4 mg/dL). Thus, 
withdrawal of an ACEI in such patients should occur only when the rise in 
creatinine exceeds 30% above baseline within the first 2 months of ACEI 
initiation, or hyperkalemia develops, ie, serum potassium level of 5.6 mmol/L or 
greater.

DOI: 10.1001/archinte.160.5.685
PMID: 10724055 [Indexed for MEDLINE]=== 28279964
1. BMJ. 2017 Mar 9;356:j791. doi: 10.1136/bmj.j791.

Serum creatinine elevation after renin-angiotensin system blockade and long term 
cardiorenal risks: cohort study.

Schmidt M(1)(2)(3), Mansfield KE(4), Bhaskaran K(4), Nitsch D(4), Sørensen 
HT(2), Smeeth L(4), Tomlinson LA(4).

Author information:
(1)Department of Non-Communicable Disease Epidemiology, London School of Hygiene 
and Tropical Medicine, London, UK morten.schmidt@clin.au.dk.
(2)Department of Clinical Epidemiology, Aarhus University Hospital, Aarhus, 
Denmark.
(3)Department of Internal Medicine, Regional Hospital of Randers, Randers, 
Denmark.
(4)Department of Non-Communicable Disease Epidemiology, London School of Hygiene 
and Tropical Medicine, London, UK.

Comment in
    BMJ. 2017 Mar 9;356:j1122. doi: 10.1136/bmj.j1122.
    Evid Based Med. 2017 Oct;22(5):185-186. doi: 10.1136/ebmed-2017-110751.

Objective To examine long term cardiorenal outcomes associated with increased 
concentrations of creatinine after the start of angiotensin converting enzyme 
inhibitor/angiotensin receptor blocker treatment.Design Population based cohort 
study using electronic health records from the Clinical Practice Research 
Datalink and Hospital Episode Statistics.Setting UK primary care, 
1997-2014.Participants Patients starting treatment with angiotensin converting 
enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (n=122 363).Main outcome 
measures Poisson regression was used to compare rates of end stage renal 
disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and death among patients with 
creatinine increases of 30% or more after starting treatment against those 
without such increases, and for each 10% increase in creatinine. Analyses were 
adjusted for age, sex, calendar period, socioeconomic status, lifestyle factors, 
chronic kidney disease, diabetes, cardiovascular comorbidities, and use of other 
antihypertensive drugs and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.Results Among 
the 2078 (1.7%) patients with creatinine increases of 30% or more, a higher 
proportion were female, were elderly, had cardiorenal comorbidity, and used 
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, loop diuretics, or potassium sparing 
diuretics. Creatinine increases of 30% or more were associated with an increased 
adjusted incidence rate ratio for all outcomes, compared with increases of less 
than 30%: 3.43 (95% confidence interval 2.40 to 4.91) for end stage renal 
disease, 1.46 (1.16 to 1.84) for myocardial infarction, 1.37 (1.14 to 1.65) for 
heart failure, and 1.84 (1.65 to 2.05) for death. The detailed categorisation of 
increases in creatinine concentrations (<10%, 10-19%, 20-29%, 30-39%, and ≥40%) 
showed a graduated relation for all outcomes (all P values for trends <0.001).

across subgroups of patients, and among continuing users.Conclusions Increases 
in creatinine after the start of angiotensin converting enzyme 
inhibitor/angiotensin receptor blocker treatment were associated with adverse 
cardiorenal outcomes in a graduated relation, even below the guideline 
recommended threshold of a 30% increase for stopping treatment.

second and third trimesters of pregnancy is contraindicated because of their 
association with an increased risk of fetopathy. In contrast, first-trimester 
use of ACE inhibitors has not been linked to adverse fetal outcomes. We 
conducted a study to assess the association between exposure to ACE inhibitors 
during the first trimester of pregnancy only and the risk of congenital 
malformations.

and born between 1985 and 2000 for whom there was no evidence of maternal 
diabetes. We identified 209 infants with exposure to ACE inhibitors in the first 
trimester alone, 202 infants with exposure to other antihypertensive medications 
in the first trimester alone, and 29,096 infants with no exposure to 
antihypertensive drugs at any time during gestation. Major congenital 
malformations were identified from linked vital records and hospitalization 
claims during the first year of life and confirmed by review of medical records.
RESULTS: Infants with only first-trimester exposure to ACE inhibitors had an 
increased risk of major congenital malformations (risk ratio, 2.71; 95 percent 
confidence interval, 1.72 to 4.27) as compared with infants who had no exposure 
to antihypertensive medications. In contrast, fetal exposure to other 
antihypertensive medications during only the first trimester did not confer an 
increased risk (risk ratio, 0.66; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.25 to 1.75).

the cardiovascular system (risk ratio, 3.72; 95 percent confidence interval, 
1.89 to 7.30) and the central nervous system (risk ratio, 4.39; 95 percent 
confidence interval, 1.37 to 14.02).
CONCLUSIONS: Exposure to ACE inhibitors during the first trimester cannot be 
considered safe and should be avoided.

OBJECTIVE: To examine a reported association between use of angiotensin 
converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors during the first trimester and risk of 
malformations in offspring.
DESIGN: A population based, retrospective cohort study linking automated 
clinical and pharmacy databases including comprehensive electronic medical 
records.
PARTICIPANTS: Pregnant women and their live born offspring (465,754 
mother-infant pairs) in the Kaiser Permanente Northern California region from 
1995 to 2008.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE: Congenital malformation in live births.
RESULTS: The prevalence of ACE inhibitor use in the first trimester only was 
0.9/1000, and the use of other antihypertensive medications was 2.4/1000. After 
adjustment for maternal age, ethnicity, parity, and obesity, use of ACE 
inhibitors during the first trimester only seemed to be associated with 
increased risk of congenital heart defects in offspring compared with normal 
controls (those with neither hypertension nor use of any antihypertensives 
during pregnancy) (15/381 (3.9%) v 6232/400,021 (1.6%) cases, odds ratio 1.54 
(95% confidence interval 0.90 to 2.62)). A similar association was observed for 
use of other antihypertensives (28/1090 (2.6%) cases of congenital heart 
defects, odds ratio 1.52 (1.04 to 2.21)). However, compared with hypertension 
controls (those with a diagnosis of hypertension but without use of 
antihypertensives) (708/29,735 (2.4%) cases of congenital heart defects), 
neither use of ACE inhibitors or of other antihypertensives in the first 
trimester was associated with increased congenital heart defects risk (odds 
ratios 1.14 (0.65 to 1.98) and 1.12 (0.76 to 1.64) respectively).
CONCLUSIONS: Maternal use of ACE inhibitors in the first trimester has a risk 
profile similar to the use of other antihypertensives regarding malformations in 
live born offspring. The apparent increased risk of malformations associated 
with use of ACE inhibitors (and other antihypertensives) in the first trimester 
is likely due to the underlying hypertension rather than the medications.

BACKGROUND: Whether chlorthalidone is superior to hydrochlorothiazide for 
preventing major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with hypertension is 
unclear.
METHODS: In a pragmatic trial, we randomly assigned adults 65 years of age or 
older who were patients in the Department of Veterans Affairs health system and 
had been receiving hydrochlorothiazide at a daily dose of 25 or 50 mg to 
continue therapy with hydrochlorothiazide or to switch to chlorthalidone at a 
daily dose of 12.5 or 25 mg. The primary outcome was a composite of nonfatal 
myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure resulting in hospitalization, 
urgent coronary revascularization for unstable angina, and non-cancer-related 
death. Safety was also assessed.
RESULTS: A total of 13,523 patients underwent randomization. The mean age was 72 
years. At baseline, hydrochlorothiazide at a dose of 25 mg per day had been 
prescribed in 12,781 patients (94.5%). The mean baseline systolic blood pressure 
in each group was 139 mm Hg. At a median follow-up of 2.4 years, there was 
little difference in the occurrence of primary-outcome events between the 
chlorthalidone group (702 patients [10.4%]) and the hydrochlorothiazide group

any of the components of the primary outcome. The incidence of hypokalemia was 
higher in the chlorthalidone group than in the hydrochlorothiazide group (6.0% 
vs. 4.4%, P<0.001).

commonly used in clinical practice, patients who received chlorthalidone did not 
have a lower occurrence of major cardiovascular outcome events or 
non-cancer-related deaths than patients who received hydrochlorothiazide.

Diuretic therapy for hypertension and the risk of primary cardiac arrest.

Siscovick DS(1), Raghunathan TE, Psaty BM, Koepsell TD, Wicklund KG, Lin X, Cobb 
L, Rautaharju PM, Copass MK, Wagner EH.

(1)Department of Medicine, University of Washington, Seattle.

Comment in
    N Engl J Med. 1994 Jun 30;330(26):1899-900. doi: 
10.1056/NEJM199406303302613.

BACKGROUND: The results of trials of the primary prevention of coronary heart 
disease have suggested that treating hypertension with high doses of thiazide 
diuretic drugs might increase the risk of sudden death from cardiac causes. In 
contrast, treatment with low doses of thiazide reduces the risk of coronary 
heart disease.
METHODS: To examine the association between thiazide treatment for hypertension 
and the occurrence of primary cardiac arrest, we conducted a population-based 
case-control study among enrollees of a health maintenance organization. The 
case patients were 114 persons with hypertension who had a primary cardiac 
arrest from 1977 through 1990. The control patients were a stratified random 
sample of 535 persons with hypertension. The patients' treatment was assessed 
with the use of a computerized pharmacy data base. Records of their ambulatory 
care were reviewed to determine other clinical characteristics.
RESULTS: The risk of primary cardiac arrest among patients receiving combined 
thiazide and potassium-sparing diuretic therapy was lower than that among 
patients treated with a thiazide without potassium-sparing therapy (odds ratio, 
0.3; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.1 to 0.7). As compared with low-dose 
thiazide therapy (25 mg daily), moderate-dose therapy (50 mg daily) was 
associated with a moderate increase in risk (odds ratio, 1.7; 95 percent 
confidence interval, 0.7 to 4.5), and high-dose therapy (100 mg daily) was 
associated with a larger increase in risk (odds ratio, 3.6; 95 percent 
confidence interval, 1.2 to 10.8) (P value for trend, 0.02). The addition of a 
potassium-sparing drug to low-dose thiazide therapy was associated with a 
reduced risk of cardiac arrest (odds ratio, 0.4; 95 percent confidence interval, 
0.1 to 1.5).
CONCLUSIONS: Both the dose of thiazide drugs and the addition of 
potassium-sparing drugs influence the risk of primary cardiac arrest. These 
results may explain the differences in the effect of antihypertensive therapy on 
mortality from coronary heart disease in previous clinical trials.
